senses.gloss: To take money or an advantage from someone by tricking them.
examples: That shop *cheats* tourists every summer.
The broker *cheated* investors out of millions.
Customers felt *cheated* when the refund never came.

senses.gloss: To be unfaithful to a husband, wife, or partner.
examples: He swore he would never *cheat*.
She *cheated* on her first husband for two years.
They split up after she found out he had been *cheating*.

senses.gloss: To mark a box or an item with a check mark.
examples: *Check* the box if you want a receipt.
She *checked* each item on the list as she packed it.
Two of the three boxes were already *checked*.

senses.gloss: To hand a bag or a coat over to an airline, a hotel, or a cloakroom so that it is carried or kept for you.
examples: Do you want to *check* that bag or carry it on?
We *checked* two suitcases in Denver.
My coat is *checked* at the front desk.

senses.gloss: To stop something from spreading or getting worse.
examples: Vaccines *check* the spread of the disease.
The new rules *checked* the rise in rents.
The fire was finally *checked* at the ridge.

senses.gloss: To relax and do nothing, in informal speech.
examples: We're just going to *chill* at home tonight.
They *chilled* on the porch all afternoon.
I was *chilling* in my room when she called.

senses.gloss: To squeeze someone's throat so that they cannot breathe.
examples: Loosen that collar before it *chokes* the dog.
The wrestler *choked* his opponent until the referee stepped in.
The dog had been *choking* itself pulling against the leash.

senses.gloss: To fail at the important moment because of nerves.
senses.ru: сдавать (о нервах), оплошать в решающий момент
examples: Great players don't *choke* in the last minute.
He *choked* and missed both free throws.
Our team has *choked* in the playoffs three years running.

senses.gloss: To fill a space so completely that nothing can move through it.
senses.ru: забивать, заполнять до отказа; заглушать (о сорняках)
examples: Weeds *choke* the flower beds every August.
Traffic *choked* the tunnel for two hours.
The creek was *choked* with fallen branches.

senses.gloss: Of a train or an engine, to move along making a heavy, repeated sound.
examples: Old tractors *chug* up that hill all summer.
The train *chugged* out of the station right on time.
A little boat was *chugging* across the bay.

senses.gloss: To draw a ring around something on paper.
examples: *Circle* the correct answer.
She *circled* two dates on the calendar.
Every typo was *circled* in red ink.

senses.gloss: Of blood, air, or water, to move continuously through a system.
examples: Blood *circulates* through the body about once a minute.
The fan *circulated* warm air into the back rooms.
Cool water has been *circulating* through the pipes all night.

senses.gloss: To move around a room talking to one person after another.
senses.ru: обходить гостей, общаться с разными людьми (на приёме)
examples: A good host *circulates* instead of sitting down.
She *circulated* among the guests with a tray.
He spent the evening *circulating* and handing out cards.

senses.gloss: To mention something as a reason or an example.
senses.ru: ссылаться на (причину), приводить как пример, указывать
examples: Officials *cite* the weather as the main cause.
She *cited* family reasons when she resigned.
Rising rent is often *cited* as the reason small stores close.

senses.gloss: To give someone an official ticket or an order to appear in court for breaking a law.
senses.ru: выписывать штраф, привлекать к ответственности; вызывать в суд
examples: Officers can *cite* you for parking there.
The inspector *cited* the landlord twice last year.
The restaurant was *cited* for three health violations.

senses.gloss: To officially ask for money or property that you have a right to.
senses.ru: требовать, востребовать; получать по праву, оформлять (возврат)
examples: You can *claim* a refund within thirty days.
She *claimed* the prize the next morning.
Nobody has *claimed* the wallet that was turned in.

senses.gloss: Of an accident or a disaster, to take someone's life.
examples: House fires *claim* hundreds of lives every winter.
The storm *claimed* four lives in one county.
The crash has *claimed* a fifth victim.

senses.gloss: To fight or argue openly with someone.
examples: The two senators *clash* over spending every year.
Protesters *clashed* with police downtown.
The coach and the owner have *clashed* repeatedly this season.

senses.gloss: To hold something tightly in your hand or your arms.
examples: She *clasps* her hands whenever she is nervous.
He *clasped* my hand and thanked me twice.
The child was *clasping* a stuffed rabbit.

senses.gloss: To declare officially that information is secret.
examples: The agency can *classify* anything it calls sensitive.
The Pentagon *classified* the report for thirty years.
Most of the file is still *classified*.

senses.gloss: Of the sky or the weather, to become bright and free of clouds, fog, or rain.
examples: The sky usually *clears* by noon here.
The fog *cleared* just before we landed.
The storm has *cleared*, and the stars are out.

senses.gloss: To prove that someone is not guilty.
examples: New evidence may *clear* him.
The jury *cleared* her of all charges.
He was *cleared* after two years in prison.

senses.gloss: To give official permission or approval for something.
examples: A doctor has to *clear* you before you can play again.
The tower *cleared* us for takeoff.
The drug has not been *cleared* for children.

senses.gloss: To make a short, sharp sound.
examples: The lock *clicks* when it is fully shut.
Her heels *clicked* down the hallway.
Something was *clicking* under the hood the whole way home.

senses.gloss: To suddenly become clear or make sense.
examples: A rule doesn't always *click* until you use it.
Then it *clicked*: I had met him at the wedding.
Nothing was *clicking* for me in that class.

senses.gloss: To like someone immediately and get along with them easily.
examples: Some roommates just *click*.
We *clicked* the first time we met.
They have never really *clicked* as a team.

senses.gloss: To hit someone hard, in informal speech.
examples: Say that again and he'll *clock* you.
The guy *clocked* him in the jaw.
I got *clocked* by a stray elbow under the basket.

senses.gloss: Of a store or a business, to stop serving customers for the day, or to shut down for good.
examples: The pharmacy *closes* at nine.
The factory *closed* in 2008 and never reopened.
Three branches have *closed* since January.

senses.gloss: To finish and settle a sale or a business deal.
examples: A good agent can *close* almost any sale.
We *closed* on the house in June.
The deal was *closed* late Friday afternoon.

senses.gloss: To make someone's thinking or judgment less clear.
examples: Fear can *cloud* your judgment.
Anger *clouded* his thinking that night.
He admitted that grief had *clouded* the decision.

senses.gloss: To help an enemy army that has taken control of your country.
examples: Villagers who *collaborate* face harsh punishment.
Some officials *collaborated* simply to keep their jobs.
He was accused of having *collaborated* with the occupiers.

senses.gloss: Of a person, to fall down suddenly from illness or exhaustion.
senses.ru: падать без сил, свалиться; терять сознание
examples: Runners sometimes *collapse* in the last mile.
He *collapsed* at his desk and was rushed to the hospital.
She has *collapsed* twice this month.

senses.gloss: Of a plan, a business, or a system, to fail suddenly and completely.
examples: Talks can *collapse* over a single word.
The company *collapsed* after the fraud came out.
Home prices have *collapsed* in some cities.

senses.gloss: To fold something into a smaller shape for carrying or storing.
examples: The stroller *collapses* with one hand.
He *collapsed* the tripod and put it in the trunk.
The table can be *collapsed* and stored under the bed.

senses.gloss: To influence the way someone sees or judges something, usually unfairly.
examples: Don't let one bad review *color* your opinion.
His childhood *colored* everything he wrote.
The report was *colored* by the author's politics.

senses.gloss: To search a place very carefully and completely.
examples: Volunteers *comb* the beach after every storm.
Detectives *combed* the apartment for fingerprints.
We have *combed* the records twice and found nothing.

senses.gloss: To be important or valuable enough to get respect, attention, or a high price.
examples: Few teachers *command* that kind of respect.
The painting *commanded* four million dollars at auction.
Her work has *commanded* attention since her first show.

senses.gloss: To change a criminal's punishment to a lighter one.
examples: Only the governor can *commute* a death sentence.
The president *commuted* her sentence to time served.
His sentence was *commuted* after twelve years.

senses.gloss: To balance out a weakness or a loss by doing something else.
examples: A good lens can *compensate* for poor light.
She *compensated* for a thin résumé with a strong interview.
The engine runs rough, and the computer is constantly *compensating* for it.

senses.gloss: To turn written code into a program that a computer can run.
examples: The project *compiles* in under a minute.
I *compiled* it twice and got the same error.
The app has to be *compiled* before you can test it.

senses.gloss: To be the parts that something is made of.
examples: Two small islands *compose* the entire country.
Farmers *composed* most of the population back then.
The board is *composed* of five parents and two teachers.

senses.gloss: To make yourself calm again after being upset.
senses.ru: успокаиваться, брать себя в руки, взять себя в руки
examples: Give her a minute to *compose* herself.
He *composed* himself and started the speech again.
She spoke slowly, *composing* herself between sentences.

senses.gloss: To put something at risk or weaken it, especially safety, secrecy, or health.
examples: One careless email can *compromise* the whole system.
The leak *compromised* two undercover agents.
Your password may have been *compromised*.

senses.gloss: To admit publicly that you have lost an election or a contest.
examples: He refused to *concede* until every vote was counted.
She *conceded* on Wednesday morning.
Neither candidate has *conceded* yet.

senses.gloss: To become pregnant.
examples: Many couples *conceive* within a year of trying.
She *conceived* shortly after the treatment.
The twins were *conceived* through IVF.

senses.gloss: To gather in one place in large amounts, or to bring things together in one place.
examples: Most of the new jobs *concentrate* in two counties.
The company *concentrated* its factories in the South.
Wealth has become *concentrated* in a handful of cities.

senses.gloss: To bring something to an end, or to come to an end.
examples: We usually *conclude* the meeting with questions.
The concert *concluded* with an encore.
The trial has *concluded* after six weeks.

senses.gloss: To formally arrange and finish an agreement.
examples: The two countries hope to *conclude* a trade deal this year.
They *concluded* an agreement in March.
A cease-fire was *concluded* on Friday.

senses.gloss: To give someone a punishment, especially in a court of law.
examples: No judge wants to *condemn* a teenager to life in prison.
The court *condemned* him to death in 1962.
They were *condemned* to hard labor.

senses.gloss: To declare officially that a building is too unsafe to be used.
senses.ru: признавать аварийным (здание), признать непригодным для жилья
examples: The city can *condemn* any building without a fire escape.
Inspectors *condemned* the old school last spring.
The house has been *condemned* and will be torn down.

senses.gloss: Of steam or a gas, to turn into liquid on a cool surface.
examples: Steam *condenses* on the bathroom mirror.
Moisture *condensed* inside the windows overnight.
Water had *condensed* on the cold pipe and dripped onto the floor.

senses.gloss: To train a person or an animal to react in a certain way automatically.
senses.ru: приучать, приучить; вырабатывать рефлекс, формировать привычку
examples: Ads *condition* kids to want the newest thing.
Pavlov *conditioned* dogs to salivate at the sound of a bell.
We have been *conditioned* to check our phones every few minutes.

senses.gloss: To put conditioner on your hair.
examples: I shampoo and *condition* twice a week.
She washed and *conditioned* her hair before the party.
*Conditioning* your hair helps with tangles.

senses.gloss: To carry out or organize an activity such as a study, a search, or an interview.
examples: Researchers *conduct* the survey every spring.
Police *conducted* a search of the garage.
The interviews were *conducted* by phone.

senses.gloss: Of a material, to let heat or electricity pass through it.
examples: Copper *conducts* electricity better than steel.
The metal handle *conducted* the heat straight to his hand.
Salt water is very good at *conducting* electricity.

senses.gloss: To behave in a particular way.
examples: Jurors must *conduct* themselves carefully outside the courtroom.
He *conducted* himself well under pressure.
She was praised for how she had *conducted* herself during the hearing.

senses.gloss: To talk something over with other people before deciding.
examples: Let me *confer* with my partner and call you back.
The referees *conferred* for a full minute.
The judges have been *conferring* since lunch.

senses.gloss: Of a legislature, to approve someone's appointment to an office.
examples: The Senate has to *confirm* every federal judge.
Lawmakers *confirmed* her as attorney general.
He was *confirmed* by a single vote.

senses.gloss: To feel that you understand and like another person.
senses.ru: находить общий язык, сближаться; устанавливать контакт
examples: Good teachers *connect* with their students.
We *connected* right away.
He has never really *connected* with his stepfather.

senses.gloss: To succeed in dealing with a fear, a problem, or a difficulty.
examples: Nobody *conquers* jet lag on the first day.
She *conquered* her fear of flying last year.
The disease has not been *conquered* yet.
